senses.gloss:
Gaṅgāsāgara
(‘the place [where the river] गङ्गा [joins the] sāgara or ocean’)
------------------------------------------
The river गङ्गा is undoubtedly the holiest of all the rivers of India and has been thus revered for at least five millenniums. Just as the place of its origin (Gaṅgotrī) and the various places of पिल्ग्रिमगे on its banks, even the region of its joining the ocean (the Bay of Bengal) has been considered as extremely holy. This place, known as the गङ्गासागर (and also Guhyakṣetra), was once the hermitage of the sage कपिल, who had reduced to ashes, the 60,000 sons of the king सगर. The Pāṇḍavas, during their vanavāsa or sojourn through the forests had visited this place.
The place is situated about 144 kms. (90 miles) from the Diamond Harbour which itself is 61 kms. (38 miles) from the metropolis of Calcutta. There are steamer or boat services from the harbour up to the island.
There are some old temples in the region known as Vāmankhal and Candan-pīḍi. One of them is that of the goddess Viśālākṣī.
On the occasion of मकर सङ्क्रान्ति (14th-15th January) thousands of pilgrims take bath here.
See also GAṄGĀ.

Gaṅgeśa
------------------------------------------
Gaṅgeśa, also known as गङ्गेश उपाध्याय (A. D. 1200), was the brightest luminary among the logicians of Bengal who practically started a new school called ‘Navya-न्याय’. He belonged to मिथिला (in North Bihar). He wrote only one work, the Tattvacintāmaṇi in which he has dealt with only four प्रमाणस् (means or methods of knowledge) accepted by the Nyāya-sūtras of the sage गौतम. They are: प्रत्यक्ष (direct perception), अनुमान (inference), उपमान (comparison) and शब्द (the वेदस्).
His discussions on the अनुमान aspect of knowledge received very great attention among the scholars, thus developing an entirely new school of thought. A very large number of commentaries and subcommentaries have been composed on this single work. Among them, the commentary of Raghunātha Śiromaṇi (A. D. 1500) and the subcommentaries on the same became extremely popular among the scholars of Bengal.
The contribution of this work is more in the direction of linguistic notations than in metaphysics.

Gaṅgā
(‘one who descended to this earth’)
------------------------------------------
The rivers of a country are its life-line. Hindu India has always looked upon its rivers, not as just physical or natural objects but as divinities, goddesses of prosperity.
Of all the rivers of India, no river has captivated the minds and the hearts of the people more than the river गङ्गा. For many a Hindu, a bath in it is a life-time’s ambition. No religious act can be ceremonially complete without its water being used in some form or the other. A few drops of its water poured into the mouth of a dying person will remove all the sins. Immersion of the ashes of a dead person’s body in it will give him लिबेरतिओन्.
Gaṅgā, in the Scriptures
Though the river गङ्गा has been mentioned in the Ṛgveda only once (vide Nadīstuti 10.75.5 and 6), it is the first in the list. There are references to it in other places also such as the Ṛgveda (6.45.31), the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa (13.5.4.11 and 13) and also the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa (39.9). The Rāmāyaṇa, the Mahābhārata (Anuśāsanaparva) and many पुराणस् such as the Padma, the Nāradīya, the Agni and the Matsya contain hundreds of verses eulogising the greatness and the sanctifying power of the गङ्गा river. In the Bhagavadgītā (10.31) Śrī कृष्ण identifies himself with it among all the rivers.
Gaṅgā, the Goddess
Almost all the well-known rivers of (undivided) India have a dual form and have been described in the mythological literature as deities or goddesses. Icono-graphical works even ascribe to them specific forms and give detailed descriptions. For instance the river goddess गङ्गा is pictured as a beautiful lady of white complexion riding a crocodile and holding a pot and a lotus in her two hands. If shown with four hands, she may be exhibiting the abhaya (protection) and the varada (boon-giving) mudrās also. पाश (noose) and aṅkuśa (goad) are also shown sometimes, instead of the pot and the lotus.
As per the account in the Mahābhārata (Ādiparva 96-98) गङ्गा, the river-goddess was cursed to be born as a human being in this world. The king Mahābhiṣa who had attained हेअवेन् was also cursed similarly. He was reborn as the king Śāntanu. Śāntanu married गङ्गा. भीष्म of the महाभारत fame was their last son.
Gaṅgā, the Celestial River
The river गङ्गा is said to have been born out of the left foot of विष्णु in his इन्चर्नतिओन् as वामन-त्रिविक्रम. (Hence the name ‘Viṣṇupadī.’) It was then confined to the celestial region only.
When the 60,000 sons of the king सगर of अयोध्या were reduced to ashes by the curse of the sage कपिल, a way had to be found to redeem them from their sins. Bringing the celestial river गङ्गा to this earth and making it flow on their ashes was the solution. king भगीरथ, a descendant of सगर, achieved this stupendous task by pleasing शिव through severe austerities. Thus she came to be known as ‘Bhāgīrathī’. शिव captured the celestial river that started to jump down with a terrific speed, in his matted locks and then allowed her to stream out. While flowing through the hermitage of the sage Jahnu, she flooded it, thereby provoking him to swallow it up. At the earnest entreaties of भगीरथ she was allowed to emerge from the ear of the sage. (Hence the name ‘Jāhnavī’.) She finally flowed over the ashes of सगर’s sons thereby liberating them.
Gaṅgā, the River as We Know It
Geographically speaking, the river गङ्गा takes its birth near Gaṅgotrī in the Tehri Garhwal district of Uttar Pradesh. It is then known as भागीरथी. अलकनन्दा is the second rivulet born near the Tibetan border which joins the former near Devaprayāga about 64 kms. (40 miles) from the well-known place of पिल्ग्रिमगे, हरिद्वार. At this place it enters the plains, and is called ‘Gaṅgā’ hereafter. The various tributaries that join the गङ्गा over its long course are: Mandākinī, यमुना, Ghāgrā (Sarayū), Sone, Dāmodar, Gaṇḍak and Kosī. Near the sea—the Bay of Bengal—another mighty river, the ब्रह्मपुत्र, joins it.
The total length of the river is 2500 kms. (1557 miles). It breaks into a number of branches near the sea. Hoogly and Padmā are the major branches.
गङ्गा at काशी">River गङ्गा at KāśīA good number of pilgrim centres are situated on the banks of the गङ्गा and its tributaries. They are: Devaprayāga, रुद्रप्रयाग, Karṇaprayāga, Badarī-nātha, केदारनाथ, Hṛṣīkeśa, हरिद्वार, प्रयाग and काशी (Vārāṇasī). To this list may be added Gaṅgotrī and गङ्गासागर, where it joins the sea, the Bay of Bengal.
Gaṅgāsnāna or Ritual Bath in the Gaṅgā
A bath in any river cleanses the body. But a bath in the holy river गङ्गा, that too when the proper procedure prescribed in the religious treatises is followed, purifies the मिन्द् too.
The following are the various steps given in such works (vide Matsyapurāṇa 102), to be followed by an earnest pilgrim who wishes to take a ritual bath in the holy river:
Saṅkalpa (pious resolve indicating the desire to destroy one’s sins and acquire religious merit), selecting a suitable spot in the river for taking bath uttering the famous अष्टाक्षरी-मन्त्र (Oṁ namo nārāyaṇāya), आचमन (ceremonial sipping of water), āhvāna (invitation to the river goddess to be present at that particular spot by uttering her various names such as Dakṣā, पृथ्वी, Vihagā, Amṛtā, Śivā, Kṣemā, जाह्नवी, Śāntā and so on), prokṣaṇa (sprinkling the river water on one’s head), mṛttikālepana (applying clay taken from the bottom of the river, with appropriate mantras), स्नान (bath), आचमन, wearing of clean white clothes, तर्पण (satiating the manes and other beings in all the three worlds), अर्घ्य to सूर्य (offering of water taken in the joined palms of the hand) and visiting a temple of विष्णु and returning home.
For the benefit of those who have cherished a strong desire to take a bath in the गङ्गा river, but are unable to do so due to reasons like serious illness, old-age or poverty, the पुराणस् and the धर्मशास्त्रस् have suggested an ingenious method, the ‘pratinidhi’ system. On the request made to a pilgrim who is actually going to take the bath, this pilgrim can make a small effigy of कुश grass and give it the bath with appropriate mantras that include the name of the solicitor. The latter then gets one-eighth of the religious merit he would have got if he had actually taken the bath himself.
Taking bath in the river गङ्गा on certain special days is supposed to give infinitely great religious merit. Some of these are: अमावास्या (new-मोओन् day); सङ्क्रान्ति (days of the apparent passage of the sun from one zodiacal sign to the next); days of lunar and solar eclipses; days of पुष्कर (the day on which the planet बृहस्पति or जुपितेर् enters the zodiacal sign assigned to the river गङ्गा viz., Meṣa, or Aries). The पुष्कर day for any river comes once in twelve years and the auspicious moment for a few minutes only.
Festivals Related to the Gaṅgā
An important day on which a festival called ‘Daśaharā’ is celebrated in North India, falls on Jyeṣṭha śukla daśamī (the 10th day in the bright fortnight of the month of Jyeṣṭha, usually in May). It is said to be the day on which the river गङ्गा descended to this earth. Since a bath in the river on this day, especially at the Daśāśvamedha-ghāṭ of काशी (Banaras), destroys ten types of sins it is christened ‘daśaharā’ (daśa = ten; harā = destroyer).
The biggest bathing festival connected with the river गङ्गा is the कुम्भमेला and the Ardhakumbhamelā, held respectively once in twelve years and six years at हरिद्वार (Hardwar) and at प्रयाग (modern Allahabad), in the States of Uttaranchal and Uttar Pradesh. Millions of people take bath in the river on these occasions.
Death, Last-rites and the Gaṅgā
With a rare insight into the human problem of suffering, the धर्मशास्त्रस् have permitted religious सुइचिदे in certain cases such as decrepitude brought by old-age, incurable diseases with great pain or as voluntary punishment for mortal sins. This has to be normally done by drowning oneself in the sacred river गङ्गा, especially at the त्रिवेणी-saṅgama of प्रयाग (Allahabad).
Ceremonial immersion of either the body or the ashes after च्रेमतिओन् is another practice in vogue that is said to bring great religious merit to the सोउल् of the dead person.
Conclusion
Thus it is seen that the गङ्गा has been one of the major aspects of Hindu religion and culture that has helped it to be not only alive but also vigorously active. That is why a popular saying has identified it with one of the three legs of the tripod upon which हिन्दुइस्म् stands the other two being the Gītā and the गायत्री.

Gaṅgāvataraṇa
(‘descent of [the river] गङ्गा’)
------------------------------------------
The story of भगीरथ, bringing the celestial river गङ्गा down to this earth has been described in great detail in the Rāmāyaṇa (1.43), the Bhāgavata (9.9), the Mahābhārata (Vanaparva 109) and the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa (53). This has often provided the artisans and sculptors with an inspiring theme for their work.
In महाबलिपुरम् (or Māmallā-puram) situated 50 kms. to the south of Madras (now Chennai) there is a distinguished relief work, carved into a huge rock, depicting the descent of गङ्गा on this earth. It has many details, such as अस्चेतिच्स् in prayer, pilgrims, animals of all kinds heading towards the sacred water and so on. It belongs to the 7th century A. D.
See also BHAGĪRATHA and GAṄGĀ.

Gaṅgaikoṇḍa-coḷa-puram
------------------------------------------
This place near the famous place of पिल्ग्रिमगे, चिदम्बरम् (Chidambaram), in Tamil Nadu, is now a deserted village. However, it was once the capital of the king Rājendra I (A. D. 1012-1044) of the Coḷa dynasty who had conquered a large part of the peninsular India including Ceylon (now Śrī लङ्का). His ड़थेर् had built the renowned बृहदीश्वर तेम्प्ले at Tañjāvūr (Tanjore). To commemorate his own victories and also as his offering to his God, he built another, very similar, शिव temple at his new capital. Except for the विमान (tower over the sanctum) and the maṇṭapa (large open hall) the rest of the temple is in ruins. Compared to the Tañjāvūr temple the sculptures of this temple as also the carvings are of greater excellence. Another interesting feature is that there is a separate shrine for Amman or the Divine मोथेर्, called ‘Tirukkāma-koṭṭam.’
See also BṚHADĪŚVARA TEMPLE.

Gaṅgādvāra
(‘entrance to the गङ्गा’)
------------------------------------------
